**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

As the innocent Bodhisatta faces wrongful death, Sakka intervenes, slays the wicked monarch, and places the Bodhisatta upon the throne [Fausböll 1879; Tambiah 1976]. The story closes with the identification (*samodhāna*): the unrighteous king was Devadatta, Sakka was Anuruddha, Sujātā was Rāhulamātā, and the Bodhisatta became the righteous ruler [Fausböll 1879].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Dutiyo bhāgo) (Atk S0513a2) (§1.1–1.4 ↔ §745–746)
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus automated text reuse database — Internal Pali text reuse matches with the Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā
- [Fausböll 1879] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka together with its Commentary, Vol. 2 (1879) — Pali text framing, verse opening, plot resolution, and samodhāna identifications
- [Tambiah 1976] S. J. Tambiah, World Conqueror and World Renouncer (1976) — Analysis of Sakka's intervention and the declaration on righteous kingship
- [McDermott 1977] James P. McDermott, 'Is There Group Karma in Theravāda Buddhism?' (1977) — Discussion of the king's unrighteousness causing famine and pestilence, and its connection to overflow karma
- [Holt et al. 2003] John Clifford Holt, Jacob N. Kinnard, and Jonathan S. Walters, Constituting Communities (2003) — Discussion of McDermott's interpretation of overflow karma in the Jātaka
